newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asia Metals--Japan market quiet, eyes port strike.
newsitem.headline: Asia Metals--Japan market quiet, eyes port strike.

text.p: Japan's physical metals trade has been quiet in the past week, traders said on Wednesday, although they were monitoring a Japanese port strike that has potential, albeit slight, to disrupt supplies of some metals.

Two unions comprising almost half of Japan's 100,000 dock workers launched a one-day strike on Wednesday and will cease their two-year-old practice of working on Sundays, to protest U.S. demands that Japan liberalise its port practices.

Although traders said the unions' actions so far were not likely to affect metal supplies significantly, any extended strike later this month could delay shipments due to arrive by April 1 under a tariff exemption scheme.

Refined zinc imports under the scheme were expected to be particularly heavy this year at 80,000 tonnes or more, traders said, as domestic supplies have been tight amid strong demand for galvanised steel from the car and construction sectors.
Labour union officials said on Wednesday they may stage another strike depending on how deregulation proceeds.
Traders saw only a remote chance of a lengthy strike, however, with one noting that extended work stoppages were rare in Japan.
Wednesday's strike disrupted operations of about 60 Japanese vessels and an estimated 70 foreign vessels, according to the Japanese Shipowners' Association.

In the aluminium market, traders noted some Japanese buying on Tuesday, mostly for the second quarter, after London Metal Exchange three-month prices slumped to nearly $1,650 a tonne. In the previous week prices rallied to a 14-month high of $1,701.

Premiums remained firm, in line with rising U.S. premiums, although end-users continued to resist the higher levels. Traders said domestic premiums were still about $10 a tonne below those for imports.
Traders also downplayed any likely impact on the market from the current controversy over foreign involvement in the Russian aluminium industry.

One trader said the Russians were unlikely to take any actions that could significantly reduce exports and thus eat into foreign exchange earnings from the sector. "They have to feed themselves every day," he said.
Japan's physical copper market was quiet and likely to remain so until April or May, traders said.
They doubted the Chinese would buy copper at the recent high LME prices, with one trade house source saying the Chinese would more likely be sellers into Singapore at current levels.
